info.name: TikTok Backend - Auth, User & Video
info.description:
auth-service (8081) + user-service (8082) + video-service (8083) + interaction-service (8085).

HOW TO RUN
1. `make infra-up`, then start the services (`make run-auth`, `run-user`, `run-video`, and `run-interaction` for folder 4).
2. Import both files, select environment 'TikTok Backend - Local'.
3. Run folder '0. Setup' FIRST - it creates two verified accounts (User A and User B) and fills testUsername/userId/accessToken/accessTokenB/... Every later folder reads what Setup wrote, so folders 1/2/3 can then be run in any order.

THE ONE MANUAL STEP: OTP
Login now requires a verified email (403 EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED otherwise), so Setup has to verify both accounts, and no API ever echoes an OTP back. Read it from the auth-service console log - it prints `[DEV ONLY - REMOVE BEFORE COMMIT] verification OTP for <email> = <123456>` - and paste it into env var `otp` (User A) / `otpB` (User B) before running the two 'Verify Email' requests. Same for the reset-password OTP later. That is why the collection is NOT fully unattended in Collection Runner; run Setup request-by-request, then the rest with the Runner.

RATE-LIMIT REQUESTS
'Login - Too Many Attempts' and 'Resend Verification - Too Many Requests' are single requests meant to be fired several times in a row (Runner iterations) to trip the limiter, not one-shot.

WHY 403 AND NOT 401 FOR A MISSING TOKEN
This collection talks to the services DIRECTLY (8081/8082/8083), and none of them registers an AuthenticationEntryPoint, so Spring Security falls back to Http403ForbiddenEntryPoint: a missing, malformed, expired or blacklisted token all come back 403 with an empty body. 401 only appears where the controller/service throws it (INVALID_CREDENTIALS, INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN).

The docs/*-api.md files say 401 for the same case and are NOT wrong - they describe the path real clients take, through api-gateway :8080, which does register a RestAuthenticationEntryPoint and answers 401 with a proper {code:'UNAUTHORIZED'} envelope. Same rejection, different status and body depending on which door you knock on. If you point this collection at the gateway, expect 401 wherever a test here asserts 403.

console.log('Now read the OTP for ' + pm.environment.get('testEmailB') + ' from the auth-service log and set env var `otpB`.');

item.name: Login - Success (clears the attempt counter)

item.name: Refresh - Wrong Token Type (passing accessToken)
item.description: Both tokens are signed with the same secret; only the tokenType claim ('access' vs 'refresh') separates them, so this must be rejected.

item.name: Refresh - Success (rotates tokens)

exec: pm.test('a NEW refresh token comes back', () => pm.expect(body.data.refreshToken).to.not.eql(pm.environment.get('refreshToken')));

item.description: Saves the consumed token into {{rotatedRefreshToken}} so the replay test below can present it again.

item.name: Refresh - Replay Within Grace Window (401, session survives)
item.description: Run WITHIN 10s of 'Refresh - Success' (auth.jwt.rotation-grace-millis). Inside the grace the already-rotated token just gets a 401 - it looks exactly like a client retrying a /refresh whose response it never received. After the grace it is treated as theft instead: see the next request.

item.name: Refresh - Replay After Grace (kills every session)

exec: console.log('Every session for this user is now revoked. The current {{accessToken}} and {{refreshToken}} are dead - re-run 0. Setup / 3. Login User A.');

item.description: DESTRUCTIVE - run it MORE than 10s after 'Refresh - Success'. Presenting a rotated-but-unexpired token past the grace window is replay detection: SessionRevoker wipes all of the user's sessions (auth:blacklist:user:{userId} cut-off). Log in again before running other folders.

exec: pm.test('403 - refresh token is not an access token', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.description: The filter uses isValidAccessToken(), not isValid() - otherwise a 7-day refresh token would work as a bearer credential.

item.name: Social Login
item.description: Google + Facebook token exchange. The five 'no credentials needed' requests below run anywhere; the two marked REAL TOKEN need GOOGLE_CLIENT_IDS / FB_APP_ID / FB_APP_SECRET set on the service and a token pasted into the environment.

item.name: Google - Garbage Token (401 INVALID_SOCIAL_TOKEN)
item.description: Also proves the endpoint is permitAll: a 403 with an empty body here means SecurityConfig is missing the path, not that the token was rejected.

item.name: Google - REAL TOKEN (paste {{googleIdToken}} first)

exec: pm.test('requiresEmail is false for a verified Google address', () => pm.expect(data.requiresEmail).to.eql(false));

item.description: Run twice. The second run must NOT create a second account - check `SELECT count(*) FROM users` before and after. Registration and login are the same call.

item.name: Facebook - REAL TOKEN (paste {{fbAccessToken}} first)

exec: pm.test('requiresEmail is true only when Facebook gave no address', () => pm.expect(data.requiresEmail).to.be.a('boolean'));

item.description: Three outcomes, all correct. Address free: the account is created carrying it, unverified. Address already held by another account: 409 SOCIAL_LINK_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED and a code is mailed - finish with the link request below. No address at all: the account is created without one and requiresEmail is true.

item.name: Facebook - Confirm link (409 follow-up)

exec: pm.test('no second account - the session belongs to the existing one', () => pm.expect(data.tokens.accessToken).to.be.a('string'));

item.description: Second half of a 409 SOCIAL_LINK_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED: the same Facebook token, plus the 6-digit code mailed to the address behind it. Both are re-checked - the token proves the Facebook account, the code proves the mailbox - and only then is the identity attached to the existing account. Check `SELECT count(*) FROM users` before and after: it must not move.

item.name: Link - Validation Error (otp not 6 digits)

exec: pm.test('rejected before the provider token is even checked', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().code).to.eql('VALIDATION_ERROR'));

item.description: Runs anywhere - no provider credentials needed. Also proves /oauth/{provider}/link is permitAll: a 403 with an empty body here means SecurityConfig is missing the path. /oauth/google/link is the same code path with a different verifier, so it gets no request of its own.

exec: pm.test('403 - this endpoint is deliberately NOT permitAll', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: 3. Video Service
item.description:
video-service :8083, MongoDB. Two things to know before reading the assertions:

1. A published video starts as status=PROCESSING, not PUBLISHED. It only flips to PUBLISHED when media-worker consumes VideoPublishedEvent, transcodes, and emits VideoTranscodedEvent. With media-worker not running, videos stay PROCESSING forever - which is why the feed assertions below do not expect to find the video you just created.
2. GET /api/v1/videos/** is permitAll (anonymous feed), everything else needs a token. Visibility is enforced in the service, not the filter chain: the owner sees all of their own videos, everyone else (including anonymous) sees only status=PUBLISHED AND visibility=PUBLIC - anything else is a 404, never a 403, so a private video's existence is not leaked.

item.name: Upload URL
item.description: Step 1 of publishing: POST /upload-url, PUT the file bytes straight to MinIO with the presigned URL, then Publish with rawFileUrl = the returned fileUrl. The bytes never pass through video-service.

item.name: Upload URL - No Token (403)
item.description: POST is not in the permitAll GET matcher.

item.name: Upload URL - Unsupported Type (400)
item.description: Only video/mp4, video/quicktime and video/webm are accepted, and the refusal comes before the client spends a minute uploading.

item.name: Upload URL - Success (saves {{rawFileUrl}})

exec: pm.test('fileUrl is an s3 URI in the allowed bucket', () => pm.expect(data.fileUrl).to.match(/^s3:\/\/video-media\/raw\//));
// fileUrl, never uploadUrl: the presigned signature expires in minutes and fails @ValidMediaUrl on Publish.

item.description: Requires MinIO running (make infra-up). To finish the upload by hand: PUT the file to {{uploadUrl}} with header Content-Type: video/mp4 and NO Authorization header - the signature is already in the query string, and an extra Authorization header makes S3 reject it.

item.name: Publish - No Token (403)
item.description: POST is not in the permitAll GET matcher.

item.name: Publish - Validation Error (blank title, missing visibility)
item.description: title @NotBlank max 150, description max 2000, visibility @NotNull.

item.name: Publish - Rejected rawFileUrl (foreign https host)
item.description: rawFileUrl goes into VideoPublishedEvent and media-worker then FETCHES it, so an unchecked value is a URL the client picks and our backend requests. @ValidMediaUrl(schemes={https,s3}) allows only app.media.allowed-hosts (cdn.tiktok-clone.local) / allowed-buckets (video-media).

item.name: Publish - Rejected rawFileUrl (wrong s3 bucket)
item.description: For s3:// the authority is matched against allowed-buckets, not allowed-hosts.

item.name: Publish - Success (PUBLIC)

exec: pm.test('hlsUrl not set until media-worker transcodes', () => pm.expect(data.hlsUrl).to.be.oneOf([null, undefined]));

item.description: User B asking for A's PUBLIC-but-still-PROCESSING video. Once media-worker transcodes it to PUBLISHED this same request returns 200 - that difference is the point.

item.description: No token at all. The endpoint is permitAll, so this reaches the service with requesterId=null and falls to the stranger branch - 404, not 403.

Get Feed - Anonymous (200)

exec: pm.test('200 OK without a token', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('cursor page shape - items + nextCursor, no totals', () => {
pm.test('feed contains only PUBLISHED + PUBLIC videos', () => {

item.description: First page = no cursor at all. Sorted createdAt DESC then _id DESC, served by feed_idx - the same compound key the cursor encodes. The video you just published is NOT here - it is still PROCESSING until media-worker transcodes it. An empty feed on a fresh database is the expected result, not a failure; nextCursor is null there and feedCursor is stored empty.

item.name: Get Feed - Next Page via Cursor

exec: // Nothing to page through when the previous request already ended the feed.

item.description: Pass the previous response's nextCursor back verbatim - it is opaque, do not parse it or build one. nextCursor === null is the only end-of-feed signal; there is no totalPages to compare against. Because the cursor anchors on the last video of the previous page, videos published mid-scroll no longer shift items into a page already read - the exact bug the old ?page=N feed had.

item.name: Get Feed - Invalid Cursor (400)
item.description: A cursor this server did not issue is rejected loudly instead of being read as page one - a client that silently restarted from the top here would scroll in circles forever. Client fix: drop the stored cursor and reload the feed.

item.name: Get Feed - Pagination Cap Test (size=99999)
item.description: The feed clamps size itself now (VideoServiceImpl.clampSize) - it no longer goes through Pageable. /users/{userId} still does, via PageableConfig. Manual counterpart of VideoControllerPageSizeTest; needs more than 50 published videos to actually catch a regression.

item.description: User B deleting A's video. Note this one IS a 403 with a code, unlike the read path's 404: the caller already knows the id, so there is nothing left to hide.

item.description: Sets deletedAt; the document stays in Mongo.

item.name: 4. Interaction Service
item.description: interaction-service :8085, Cassandra + Redis. Only the view flow is covered here. A view is counted once per playback: the client sends the playId it generated when playback started, interaction-service claims it in Redis, and only a first claim moves the counter and emits interaction.view-events, which video-service consumes to move Video.viewCount. Replays count again; per-viewer plays are capped at 60/hour. Run '3. Video Service > Publish > Publish - Success (PUBLIC)' first - these requests read {{videoId}}.

item.name: View - No Token (403)
item.description: The per-viewer rate limit is what keeps a counted-every-play number honest, so an anonymous view has no identity to limit against - the endpoint requires a token on purpose.

item.name: View - First Time (counted)

exec: // A fresh playId means a fresh playback: this is what makes the view count again.

item.description: First request carrying this playId: the Redis claim wins, the counter moves, and VideoViewedEvent is published.

item.name: View - Same playId Again (retry, not counted)

exec: pm.test('not counted a second time', () => pm.expect(data.counted).to.be.false);

item.description: Same playId as the previous request, i.e. a client retrying a request whose response it never saw. counted=false is the normal answer, not an error - a flaky network must not read as popularity.

item.name: View - Replay (counted again)

exec: // A fresh playId means a fresh playback: this is what makes the view count again.

item.description: The same viewer playing the video a second time. A new playId, so it counts again - views are per playback, the way the number is read everywhere.

item.name: View - Different User (counted again)

exec: pm.test('counted for the second viewer', () => pm.expect(data.counted).to.be.true);

item.description: The claim is keyed on the viewer as well as the playId, so user B's view counts even while reusing user A's playId - the playId is untrusted input. Needs '0. Setup > 6. Login User B'.

item.name: Counts - includes viewCount
item.description: Public endpoint, cached in Redis for 300s and invalidated on every counted view.

item.name: Watch - Completed Session
item.description: One finished playback session. 95% counts as completed - the threshold is 90%, because players stop reporting a frame or two short of the end.

item.name: Watch - Abandoned Session
item.description: The negative label: the viewer scrolled away after two seconds.

item.name: Watch - Impossible Watch Time Is Clamped
item.description: watchedMs is client-supplied. Unclamped, an hour claimed on a ten-second video would be the highest completion ratio in the training set - exactly the row a ranker learns hardest from.

item.name: Watch - Same Viewer Again Still Counts

exec: pm.test('a rewatch is still a session', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().data.completed).to.be.true);

item.description: Every session is published, replays included: a rewatch is the strongest positive signal there is.

item.description: Anonymous playback produces no label: there is no viewer to attribute it to.

item.description: Trending is the same list for everybody, so it needs no token - a signed-out home screen still has something to show. May legitimately be empty on a fresh Redis.

exec: pm.test('200 OK, not a validation error', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Feed - Success

exec: // Kept for the paging request below, which asserts the next call does not repeat these.

item.description: Ids and a score, never video content: this service has no read path into video-service's data. The client takes these ids and fetches whatever it does not already hold.

item.name: Feed - Second Call Does Not Repeat The First
item.description: Run straight after 'Feed - Success'. This is the whole of pagination: there is no cursor and no offset, because the ranking is recomputed every request and the scores move between calls -- an offset into a ranked list would both repeat and skip. What makes the next call different is that the previous one recorded what it handed out and suppresses it for 30 minutes. Needs enough videos in the system for a second page to exist.

item.name: Feed - No Token (401)
item.description: The feed is per-viewer, so there is nothing to return without an identity.

item.name: Feed - A Watched Video Stops Being Served

// only thing that tells this service the video has been seen. Kafka delivery is async,
// so allow a second before running this.

item.description: The single most visible way a feed can look broken: serving back the video someone just finished. Nothing but POST /watch marks a video as seen.
